title: US flight outage: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop; Trump officials suggest new tech overwhelmed old equipment – as it happened
author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell and Taz Ali
text:
Good morning, and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Barely a week after sweeping to a stunning midterm victory, Democrats have found themselves facing an altogether different battle, one within their own ranks.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has launched a challenge to Chuck Schumer, of New York, for the Senate’s top Democratic leadership post. Announcing his decision during an interview with MS Now last night, Van Hollen argued that last week’s midterm election results showed Americans wanted a fundamental change in Washington, and that Democrats needed new leadership in order to deliver that.

We saw a huge outburst of democracy on election day – red states, blue states, purple states – and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption, his wars and his cruelty, it was also about a call for a larger change, to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favour of the very wealthy against working people, and it’s fuelled by a corrupt political system.

The call was to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual, and to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

His challenge came just days after Democrats secured control of the Senate, winning at least 55 seats in what has been a remarkable election cycle for the party. Winning the leadership contest requires a majority of the caucus, about 28 or 29 senators, with an election scheduled for next month.

The caucus votes behind closed doors by secret ballot, but Van Hollen told MS Now that he had the support of “more than 10” Democratic senators.

Progressive heavyweight Bernie Sanders , an independent senator from Vermont who caucuses with the Democrats, has already publicly declared he will not support Schumer , saying “the time is now for change”. Endorsing Van Hollen, Sanders said : “The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families.”

Incoming Democratic senator Abdul El-Sayed, of Michigan, has also openly backed Van Hollen , saying he was “proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority”.

The American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership. I called [Van Hollen] to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now.”

Responding to Van Hollen’s leadership bid , Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since January 2017, said he welcomed “a discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead”, but that he had the votes to be re-elected as leader.

title: All passengers and crew accounted for after New Orleans boat crash in ‘miracle on the Mississippi’
author: Ramon Antonio Vargas and Lucy Campbell in New Orleans
text:
No passengers or crew killed or critically hurt after tanker collides with river cruise ship on Mississippi, officials say

In what the city’s mayor declared a “miracle on the Mississippi”, all passengers were accounted for – with none killed or critically hurt – after a tanker collided with a river cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon.

Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals after the Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck American Cruise Lines’s American Heritage at about 12.30pm – but none of their injuries were considered critical, New Orleans’s mayor, Helena Moreno, said at a news conference.

Zero passengers or crew members were unaccounted for, Moreno said. She attributed that fact to a hectic but effective multi-agency rescue effort after the American Heritage was struck and a number of people ended up in the river, whose waters are cold and its currents are infamously perilous.

That “truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Moreno said near the scene of the crash, as a group of fellow officials around her applauded.

The American Heritage had 197 passengers onboard when it was hit, Port of New Orleans press secretary Kimberly Curth said in a statement.

About two hours before that, the American Heritage had docked at the port to begin passenger disembarkation, Curth said.

Thirty of those reported injured were on the American Heritage, and they were said to have mostly had bumps and bruises. Two others among the injured were harbor police officers who were on the river boat after the crash participating in rescue efforts.

Officials did not immediately provide details about what caused the crash. But New Orleans’s US coast guard commander Melanie Burnham said the tanker apparently had “some type of loss of steering” – as an emergency response source had indicated earlier.

The website MarineTraffic.com showed the Atlantic Asphalt’s path was seemingly uneventful as it went around the difficult bend in the Mississippi River near New Orleans’ Algiers Point neighborhood. It had just made it past the Crescent City Connection bridge linking New Orleans’ central business district and the community’s Algiers section when it began heading generally to its starboard – or right – side.

Video provided to Guardian reporting partner WWL Louisiana showed the Atlantic Asphalt then T-boned the side of the American Heritage. The cruise ship eventually slowly rolled on to its side where it was struck, according to the video, which the CBS affiliate obtained from Barry Kern, proprietor of Mardi Gras World, a tourist attraction near the scene of the crash.

One witness, Jamie Holford, told local NBC News affiliate WDSU that it took 15 minutes “from impact to where it rolled over”.

“Surreal,” Holford said. “That’s what that was.”

Maritime law expert Martin J Davies of Tulane University told the Associated Press that local pilots are onboard ships such as the Atlantic Asphalt as they travel on the Mississippi River. Those pilots know the river’s waters and the ships they are on well, Davies said.

Davies said videos circulating online of the crash suggest there was some kind of catastrophic system failure on the tanker – and some “super bad luck” for it to strike the American Heritage as passengers disembarked.

The Atlantic Asphalt was traveling slowly against the current upriver, Davies said to the AP. He added: “For something like this to happen for an upbound ship indicates that something must have gone really badly wrong.”

Separately, Davies said to local Fox affiliate WVUE that the Atlantic Asphalt was fortunate to have not hit the Crescent City Connection , which could have endangered motorists on a two-span, cantilever, steel truss bridge that is estimated to carry about 160,000 cars daily.

“This is obviously a really bad incident,” Davies said. “But it could also have struck the bridge, which it didn’t.”

A video from WDSU showed crew members of a tugboat working to pull people in lifejackets or holding on to flotation rings out of the river. An emergency response that drew in firefighters, crews of tug vessels in the vicinity, US Coast Guard helicopter and boat personnel, as well as port and city police – among others – also helped pull out people who ended up in the water in plain view of cameras and stunned eyewitnesses.

One image on social media showed people climbing on the side of the cruise boat – specifically, on stateroom balconies – after it was struck, with chairs and tables strewn about after it evidently took on water.

Blake Paterson, an independent New Orleans journalist who publishes Perdido Street.News , interviewed 65-year-old American Heritage passenger Tamara Carrasco about what she saw at the time of the crash.

The retired Atlanta elementary school teacher told Paterson that she was dining on the first floor of the riverboat when she saw the tanker careering toward the American Heritage. The tanker dropped its anchor, and she could see its crew running away on its deck, according to what Carrasco told Paterson.

Carrasco began running to the other side of the river boat, but she was knocked to the ground when the tanker hit. She said water began pouring into the dining room, making her think it was “like the Titanic”.

An employee at the Ernest N Morial Convention Center next to the scene of Friday’s crash said she realized something was awry when she could see from her vantage point that the tip of the American Heritage was tilted. She then grasped the nature of situation when she heard desperate shrieks.

“People were screaming for help,” said the employee, who asked to not be named. She recalled how she and colleagues assembled wheelchairs, water and other items in case survivors would soon need them.

Moreno said many people lost their IDs, car keys, cell phones and other belongings in the disaster. The mayor said most were from out of town.…

title: Flight Canceled During the FAA Ground Stop? Here’s What to Do.
author: Christine Chung
text:
In the United States, if your flight is canceled, significantly delayed or changed , airlines will rebook you on another flight, or at the very least try to rebook you.

Airlines will do more for passengers when the cause of a delay or a cancellation is their fault. An air traffic control outage isn’t, which means that what passengers can expect right now is limited.

You’re also entitled to a refund if your flight is canceled, regardless of the reason, or if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and you decide not to take it.

But airlines won’t guarantee other amenities, such as a hotel room in the case of overnight cancellation, ground transportation, or meal vouchers.

In the case of a tarmac delay , airlines are required to provide passengers some assistance: water and a snack within two hours of the start of a tarmac delay, unless there are safety or security reasons preventing this, according to the Transportation Department. Airlines don’t have to serve a full meal.

In the United States, airlines have three hours, for domestic flights, to move the plane to a place where passengers can safely disembark. This is four hours for international flights. However, travelers who get off the plane run the risk of not being allowed back on it.

Airlines including United Airlines , Delta Air Lines , and Alaska Airlines have issued waivers allowing travelers to change or cancel their flights without incurring any change fees or fare differences.

Waiting it out at the airport in an endless line during the current ground stop may not be the best strategy for Friday, said Jamie Larounis, a travel industry analyst.

“This won’t be a quick fix,” he said, adding that flight disruptions would likely ripple into the weekend.

Mr. Larounis said the priority for affected travelers was to get on another flight that departs in several days, booking a hotel as soon as possible if stranded outside your home city, and to consider train travel, if possible.

Scott Keyes, the founder of Going.com , a website that sends alerts for travel deals, suggested workarounds to calling an airline’s general customer service line. Travelers can try calling an airline’s international hotline, which will have fewer callers. Rebooking also might be easier to do using the airline app.

“It’s a race for any remaining seats, so the sooner you’re able to rebook, the better your odds for a remaining seat,” he added.

Christine Chung is a Times reporter covering airlines and consumer travel.

title: ‘It’s frustrating’: chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt
author: Edward Helmore in New York
text:
Travelers and crew feeling ‘pissed’ or ‘lucky’ depending on level of upset amid nationwide ground stop

T he US Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights on Friday threw airports and travel plans into chaos across the country, as passengers on planes and in airport terminals were suddenly thrust into limbo.

At New York’s John F Kennedy airport, passengers found their travel plans abruptly cancelled – some even after they’d boarded.

Steve Honberger, heading home to Portland, Oregon, with his wife and daughter, said he’d been on a plane about to take off when the shutdown was announced.

“They didn’t seem to know what’s happening, and they wanted to hold off as long as possible,” Honberger said. The plane sat at the gate for an hour and 40 minutes.

They realized they were just going to be sitting at the gate, so they eventually asked to deplane and rebook.

Many still thought it worth showing up despite the uncertainty of when flights would resume. Rashid Kahn, heading for Miami, said he’d “heard about the ground stop on the news, but the airline said we might take off 10 or 11pm”.

“I am hopeful,” he added. “But maybe it’s something to do with the date. I’m not super serious, but it’s Friday the 13th.”

Tom Rolenaitis, returning a Shiba Inu show dog named Tsuki to Finland, said it was frustrating. “It’s cutting into a three-day trip and I have to get him back to his owner. We have no idea what’s happening.”

A flight attendant headed for Barcelona, who declined to give his name, said he had been told his American Airlines flight would be slightly delayed and all incoming international flights were being allowed to land.

Another crew member from the flight said cheerfully: “Things happen. Hopefully it will all be resolved.”

As the day wore on, passengers on international flights began to be boarding, prompting applause to erupt at the gates. “It’s moving, so that’s good,” said an airline representative. “But only international is going.”

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, citing a communications problems at regional air traffic control centers, according to an FAA notice. Four hours later, FAA sent out an advisory lifting the stop.

“You can’t moan about this kind of thing ... it’s such a first-world problem,” said Laura, a woman who lives in New York and was heading for San Francisco when her JetBlue flight was grounded. She still hoped her flight would go. “That what I have to figure out,” she said, sitting on the floor of the terminal.

With the lifting of the ground stop, more chaos followed. “My flight was cancelled, then I go to a kiosk, put my information in and it says I’m leaving at 3am. Then I talk to the desk and they know nothing,” said Larson Welsh, heading to Las Vegas from Paris.

The outage has nonetheless caused upheaval for thousands of passengers. There have been 10,343 flight delays within, into or out of the US so far, according to the website FlightAware, and 1,479 cancellations. More than 1,000 aircraft were bound for US when the ground stop was announced, according to Flightradar24.

Only two national ground stops have previously been issued: on 11 September 2001, after the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center; and in January 2023, after a communications failure.

The ground stop also snarled the sports world, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams stranded as they tried to reach their destinations before a big weekend of games. It also was unclear whether referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would make it on time.

Back at JFK, travelers expressed frustration and resignation.

“My flight to California was cancelled with no information and no rebooking. My flight was cancelled last night as well due to bad weather. Now I’m missing a family event,” said a man who gave his name only as Andy. “It’s frustrating. And I’m pissed.”

Honberger, meanwhile, tried to stay optimistic, saying: “There are people sitting on tarmac, so we count ourselves lucky and we were able to book ourselves a hotel for the night.”

Tom Johnson and agencies contributed reporting

title: Developer Avoided Stricter Oversight Before Fatal Building Collapse
author: Stefanos Chen, Mihir Zaveri, Amy Julia Harris, Bianca Pallaro, Dionne Searcey and William K. Rashbaum
text:
A site on Bedford Avenue in Brooklyn was under construction when a neighboring building collapsed. Credit... Dave Sanders for The New York Times

By Stefanos Chen Mihir Zaveri Amy Julia Harris Bianca Pallaro Dionne Searcey and William K. Rashbaum

New York City officials on Friday were examining whether a developer’s desire to construct a taller building in Brooklyn than had initially been approved factored in the fatal collapse of a neighboring structure earlier this week.

Records show that the city signed off on plans for a three-story, eight-unit construction project at 2625 Bedford Avenue in the Flatbush neighborhood in March 2026. But other filings reveal that, from as far back as November 2025, the developer had intended to build something much larger: It ultimately sought approval for a nine-story building with 64 apartments, a 9,000-square-foot community space and a grocery store.

The city had not approved the more ambitious plans by Wednesday, when the more than 96-year-old building next door collapsed into the construction site, killing eight people, injuring 18 more and leaving dozens displaced.

“We have approved plans for a three-story building,” Ahmed Tigani, the commissioner of the Buildings Department, said at a news conference on Friday. But, he added, “The nine-story plan is something they seek, not what they have approval for.”

The difference between the two projects could be a key to understanding what went wrong, building experts said. The developer, a limited-liability company tied to the real estate investor Robert Fischman, was excavating the Bedford Avenue site when the building fell.

Neither Mr. Fischman nor other representatives of the development company could be reached for comment on Friday, despite visits to their homes and phone calls.

title: Trump to Meet With Putin and Xi in China, With Nuclear Proliferation on the Agenda
author: Katie Rogers
text:
President Trump will have a joint meeting with Xi Jinping, China’s leader, and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia during a summit in China next week, a White House spokeswoman said on Friday.

It will be the first trilateral meeting the three leaders have held together, and the third meeting Mr. Trump has had with Mr. Xi in person this year. At the meeting with Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump plans to discuss the war against Iran, but is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.

Olivia Wales, the White House spokeswoman, said that Mr. Trump would also address the threat of nuclear proliferation . U.S. officials have expressed concerns about a steady buildup of China’s arsenal in recent years, and a U.S. nuclear arms control treaty with Russia expired in February.

“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Ms. Wales said in a telephone briefing with reporters.

Two senior administration officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the president’s travel plans, said that Mr. Trump would travel to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila early next week. The officials said he would then travel to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, where he will meet with Mr. Xi and then both Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin.

The officials said that Mr. Trump would be joined by the billionaire Elon Musk in Shenzhen, but added that Mr. Musk would not be part of the trilateral meeting.

Mr. Trump is prepared to discuss the “difficult” topic of Beijing’s nuclear arsenal with Mr. Xi, one of the officials said.

China maintains secretive nuclear facilities and is on track to have 1,000 nuclear warheads by 2030, producing the weapons at a pace that has worried U.S. officials and analysts. On the call, the administration officials said that they did not expect any agreements on nuclear proliferation, and characterized the talks as a starting point.

Mr. Trump said this week that he had no plans to discuss with Mr. Xi the scandal that had engulfed Jensen Huang, who until this week was the chief executive of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world. Mr. Huang stepped down from his role in the wake of revelations that he had engaged in extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang , a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe is an asset of Beijing.

The officials said that the matter involving Ms. Huang was a national security issue, and did not expect Mr. Trump to discuss it with Mr. Xi during a diplomatic meeting.

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

title: Trump Administration Delays Enforcement of Medicaid Work Requirement
author: Sarah Kliff and Margot Sanger-Katz
text:
The Trump administration will allow states to delay enforcement of new rules requiring low-income adults to work in order to receive Medicaid coverage, according to a letter it sent on Friday to state Medicaid directors.

The announcement, which followed a recent loss in court over a key element of the work requirement, represents a major setback for a long-sought Republican reform. It comes less than two months before the work requirements were set to begin, on Jan. 1. States can now wait until July before ending coverage for people who do not meet the work requirement, the letter said.

In the letter, Dan Brillman, who oversees Medicaid at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, acknowledged the significant burden states faced in building out new, expensive software systems to track the employment of enrollees. Hospitals have prepared massive education campaigns to help patients navigate the additional paperwork.

“We have heard directly from states about their implementation timelines, impediments to successful launches at scale,” Mr. Brillman wrote in the letter.

He added that the federal government still expected states in January to begin checking whether Medicaid enrollees are working. But for six months, they will not be required to cancel coverage for people who fail to comply, Mr. Brillman said.

The work requirement was enacted in the summer of 2025 as part of Republicans’ major tax and domestic policy legislation. It requires Medicaid enrollees without disabilities or young children to prove they worked, volunteered or attended school at least 80 hours a month in order to qualify for the program or continue enrollment in it.

title: Flights slowly resume after US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground stop
author: Abené Clayton
text:
Transportation secretary said stoppage is due to ‘communication issue’ and homeland security says there’s no indication of ‘nefarious attack’

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights in the US on Friday, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware , and throwing airports into sudden chaos.

In a post on X, Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said the stoppage is due to “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that the FAA’s technicians are looking into the matter.

A notice from the FAA said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.

Markwayne Mullin, the Department of Homeland security director, said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage do not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”.

“There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters.

After restoring communications so all airborne flights can land, Mullin said, “we’re going to continue to work to find out what the root of the cause is”.

“We’re not ruling out anything at this point,” Mullin added.

Mullin said the immediate priority was ensuring that planes still in the air would be landing safely, but that there was no clear information on how long the stoppage might last.

In a statement, the Los Angeles mayor, Karen Bass, said that she was aware of the stoppage and receiving updates on it. Los Angeles is home to LAX, the fifth-busiest airport in the US, according to the bureau of transportation statistics

“I am in close contact with leadership at Los Angeles World Airports (LAWA) to receive real-time updates and assess impacts. We will continue to monitor this evolving situation and work closely with federal and state partners.”

At Ronald Reagan Washington national airport, gate agents, along with most travelers in the terminal, refreshed their phones looking for updates, and attempted to change their flights. Nearly every seat was filled, with some people sitting on the floor and using their luggage as makeshift desks for their laptops.

On Friday evening, there was still no timeline for when flights will be allowed to resume departures. Amid the continuing confusion at US airports, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, called on the Trump administration to offer more clarity to passengers who are trying to get to their destinations.

“Americans are stuck at airports across the country. They deserve answers, clear updates, and a plan to get home safely. Instead, the Trump Administration is correcting reporters on AI’s “preferred name”. These are not serious people,” Newsom wrote in a post on X, in reference to Mullin correcting a reporter’s use of the term AI earlier in the day.

In an interview on CNN, US congressman Ro Khanna said that he is waiting to be briefed on what exactly led to the technical issues and sparked the ground stoppage and for more public-facing communications from the transportation secretary.

“There’s a lot of nervousness,” Khanna said of the feeling among passengers. “We’re waiting to be briefed in Congress about what, exactly, has happened. We just need communication from them. If they were there every hour briefing the American public, it would help and give us a sense of a timeline.”

According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages are the result of router malfunctions that are believed to have originated at Chicago Midway airport and rippled across the rest of the US.

Amid the uncertainty, San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart.

John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travelers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport.

British Airways cancelled a flight to New York that had been due to take off from Heathrow at 10.30pm on Friday night, and a spokesperson for Manchester airport confirmed three US-bound flights scheduled to leave on Saturday morning – all operated by Virgin Atlantic – were likely to be affected if the issue was not resolved soon.

A ground-stop order by the FAA requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain in the air.

This is the third time all departing flights have been grounded in the US. The first time was on 11 September 2001; the other was in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours after a pilot notification system malfunctioned.

The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data.

Last week, the FAA announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US were officially operational in Alaska and Florida, as part of a modernization project intended to reduce flight delays and improve the flow of air traffic.

Last year, ​Congress ​approved $12.5bn to fix ​the FAA’s ageing communications system, and ​on Friday ‌the FAA ​and ​White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues.

title: House Democrats Open Inquiry After Incoming Lawmaker Accused of Sexual Harassment
author: Emily Davies
text:
House Democrats are investigating Brian Poindexter, a Democrat elected last week to represent a congressional district in northeastern Ohio, after he faced an accusation of sexual harassment.

In a statement on Friday, Julie Merz, the executive director of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said the organization had “hired an independent, third-party firm to investigate any instance of inappropriate behavior, conduct interviews and gather the facts.”

Ms. Merz said the committee, which is the House Democratic campaign arm, would have more to say after the investigation was completed.

The investigation follows an allegation that surfaced late in the race from a woman Mr. Poindexter’s campaign described as a “volunteer.” An advocacy organization for victims of sexual misconduct described the woman as a “low-level campaign staffer.” Neither the organization nor the D.C.C.C. has specified the nature of the allegation, and the woman has not been identified.

Mr. Poindexter defeated Representative Max Miller, a Republican whose ex-wife accused him of physically abusing her and their young daughter. Mr. Miller denied the accusations, which were a focal point in the campaign.

title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that blocked takeoffs for hours
author: Richard Lawler
text:
A communications problem is reportedly affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

A communications problem is reportedly affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” while planes in the air will be allowed to land. The FAA tweeted just after 5PM ET that, “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.” The flight tracking site FlightAware lists 10,494 US flights as delayed and 3,396 flights canceled as of 6:16PM ET.

According to CNN , the last nationwide ground stop in 2023 lasted for about 90 minutes after the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system for pilots went down , and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001.

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Friday afternoon, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters that there is currently no reason to suspect a cyberattack or other national security threat, or any connection to the recent Microsoft Outlook outage , but that so far no cause has been ruled out for the “telecommunications outage.”

When asked about any possible connection to the cloud-based AI Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system that was activated nationwide on November 10th, he said they were looking into that. Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company that designed the system and was awarded a 12-year $875 million contract in June to deploy it, denied any connection, tweeting “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”

Mullin also said international flights and departures are being handled on a case-by-case basis, while NBC News and the New York Times report that some flights headed to Europe and Asia have taken off from Boston and New York.

Jon Ostrower of The Air Current reports that the outage began with the Chicago air traffic control center, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, and as the FAA issued a ground stop for aircraft flying east, more facilities began reporting problems. He says the problems are disrupting both the radar and radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers and pilots, while a CNN update on Friday cited an unnamed source claiming the FAA “doesn’t know yet what is going on,” with no clear answers about the cause.

title: Nvidia Scandal Prompts Questions of What It Means to Be a Spy
author: Julian E. Barnes, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan
text:
Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the center of the Nvidia spying scandal, was believed to be using her affair with Nvidia’s founder to help China get around U.S. efforts to restrict access to advanced A.I. chips, people who have read U.S. intelligence reporting said.

But there remains much that intelligence agencies are still assessing about Ms. Huang including when she began working with China’s top spy agency, whether her cooperation was willing or coerced, how much direction Beijing gave her, and how much she relayed to officials there, the people said.

Her relationship with Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday, gave her potential access to crucial information about the company’s technology, Mr. Huang’s strategic thinking and his knowledge of Washington’s debates about A.I. policy.

She also had a business interest in ensuring a flow of chips to her own company, one of a number in Southeast Asia that provided Chinese tech firms with the computing power needed to train advanced artificial intelligence models.

The aftershocks of the scandal continue to play out as President Trump prepares for a trip next week to Asia, where he is scheduled to meet with President Xi Jinping of China, who has made a top priority of catching the United States in the race for A.I. dominance.

The unknowns surrounding Ms. Huang have generated intense scrutiny of how Chinese intelligence operates, prompted questions of what it means to be a spy and given backers of Mr. Huang an opening to raise questions about the extent and nature of her role.

title: All Accounted for After Tanker Crashes Into Docked New Orleans Riverboat

Mayor Helena Moreno of New Orleans said at a news conference that all passengers of the riverboat, the American Heritage, were accounted for after the crash. A city of New Orleans spokesperson added that 32 people were at local hospitals, and one person had serious injuries.

Capt. Melanie A. Burnham, commander of Sector New Orleans for the U.S. Coast Guard, praised the work of those who rescued the ship’s passengers.

title: Stuart Bonds made ‘racist’ and ‘divisive’ comments. But One Nation is showing no sign of dumping the NSW candidate
author: Penry Buckley
text:
The former coalminer’s claim Australians are being ‘demographically replaced’ sparked wide criticism, but his party has shown no signs of dumping him

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

In a Facebook video from a Sydney anti-immigration rally on Sunday, as a man dressed like a medieval knight watches on, One Nation’s lead upper house candidate, Stuart Bonds, launches into a speech against “mass” migration.

“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” he says.

“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we [are] going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”

In an apparent allusion to the “great replacement theory” , a far-right conspiracy theory that white westerners are being actively “replaced” by minority ethnic immigrants, he continued: “That’s the socialist plan, is to destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation.”

The comments sparked a wave of criticism, but the party has shown no signs of taking Bonds off the ticket for the 2027 New South Wales state election. One Nation did, however, dump one candidate this week: the Victorian branch disendorsed a lower-house candidate over an old social media post describing Hitler as the “GOAT” , an acronym for greatest of all time.

The rally was not a one-off. On a podcast released on Monday with the rally’s organiser, the Australian Lobby Group, Bonds appeared to double down on the remarks. He did not challenge host Scott Challen’s assertion that Labor governments were building “ethnic voting blocks with Middle Eastern and subcontinent people … to stack the numbers to entrench power for themselves”, instead responding: “Mate, and that’s why we’re going to get rid of all of the multicultural grants, right?”

On Wednesday, in an interview with ABC Upper Hunter, Bonds responded to questions about his comments by citing Australian Bureau of Statistics data that shows the proportion of Australians born overseas has trended upward since the end of the second world war, from 10% in 1945 to 32% in 2025. He did not mention that the proportion of Australians born overseas was at its highest – 32.4% – in 1891, the first year of available data.

Bonds said with the Australian birthrate beneath the 2.1 required to replace the population, “I would just like to know what people assume is going to happen.”

“Where are these people going to come from?” he said.

NSW Labor pounced on the rally comments immediately, with the state’s premier, Chris Minns, calling them “frankly outrageous and racist”. The government passed motions in both houses censuring Bonds, not yet a member.

The Coalition followed four days later. On Wednesday afternoon, the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said Bonds’ language was “clearly divisive”.

But she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement with One Nation after the March state election.

“We will not form a coalition with One Nation, [but] we’ll work with anyone post-election if we’re in a minority government,” she told reporters.

The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the party to go into a Coalition with One Nation. And with the Coalition consistently polling behind One Nation, that makes Bonds not a fringe candidate, but a potentially influential figure.

The ABC’s former election analyst, Antony Green, said the remarks played straight into Labor’s hands.

“This will certainly be something the Labor party uses in all those multi-ethnic seats in Sydney,” he said – seats like those on the rural fringes of Sydney, which One Nation said it plans to target.

Indeed the deputy premier, Prue Car, who has Indian heritage and whose electorate of Londonderry is one of the seats in question, gave an impassioned critique of Bonds’ comments in question time on Tuesday.

“Who’s he [Bonds] talking about when he talks about this?” she said. “I tell you who he’s talking about – he’s talking about families like mine, and families that I represent.”

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a director of polling group Redbridge, said that while the comments likely won’t play well in Sydney seats – including alienating moderate Liberal voters worried about the party going into Coalition with One Nation – “you might be able to get away with it in certain parts of NSW”.

And Bonds, a former coalminer, has made his base in the Hunter.

Samaras said One Nation could “clean the deck” in the regions, including Labor-held seats in the Hunter, and “pretty much anything else the Coalition hasn’t got bolted down to the ground”.

The NSW One Nation leader, Mike Newman, who in September said he “made a mistake” when he told a Sydney rally he wanted to stop abortions, did not respond directly when asked if he agreed with Bonds’ comments or if he would rein in his first-placed upper house candidate.

“What I will say is that what Stuart Bonds is a patriotic Aussie. He’s a coalminer. He has very, very strong views,” he said on Tuesday.

Newman, who previously rejected claims that One Nation was racist, said on Tuesday: “What we want to do is … protect Australian values, and that is the fundamental thing that Stuart Bonds is pushing for. It’s about assimilation.”

The NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, whose parents immigrated to Australia from India in the 1970s, told the ABC that Bonds’ comments were not grounded in reality.

“I think he’s saying that there is a deliberate conspiracy to use migrants to replace the way he puts it, native-born Australians for political reasons,” Mookhey said.

The quota for election to the upper house is 4.5%, making Bonds all but guaranteed to be elected, with One Nation polling in the high 20s and low 30s in recent months.…

title: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse
author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
text:
Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas

SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket.

Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas .

The rocket, which is on its 15th flight, is composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top.

SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted, and splashed down in the sea. The cause of that diversion remains unknown.

The Starship, meanwhile, continued on sailing through space.

Friday’s test fell short of the double-catch mantle, but the flight is poised to mark another milestone for the company. If all goes to plan, it would be the first time SpaceX has caught the rocket’s 171ft upper stage.

Previous tests focused on the retrieval of the booster.

SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk has sought to advance Starship’s “rapid reusability”, which he hopes will take humans to the moon and, controversially, to Mars.

Nasa has contracted Space X, along with Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin, to provide the lunar landers that will return astronauts to the moon in 2028.

SpaceX has launched a flurry of test flights, in recent years, some of which have resulted in explosions that signaled major design flaws.

In September, the most recent flight test, SpaceX notched a victory, sending the spacecraft into Earth’s orbit for the first time , although its engine failed during the ascent.

title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
author: Eric Berger
text:
STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.

The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase.

The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit.

title: Jewish Heirs Challenge Sale of $180 Million van Gogh Painting at Sotheby’s
author: Catherine Hickley
text:
The heirs of the Jewish former owner of an important painting by Vincent van Gogh have asked Sotheby’s to withdraw the work from sale just days before it was to be auctioned in Manhattan, arguing that it was sold under duress in 1936 as a consequence of persecution by the Nazis.

The 1890 painting, “Châtaigniers en Fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees),” carries an estimate of $180 million, the highest for any lot at this season’s art auctions, and higher than any price ever paid at auction for a work by Van Gogh. The artist painted it in Auvers-sur-Oise, near Paris, after spending two years in the south of France. The work, which is the centerpiece of the marquee fall auctions coming up next week, is backed by a financial guarantee from Sotheby’s.

The heirs, who live in the United States, say the painting was sold in Amsterdam before the Second World War as a result of financial losses sustained by their family’s publishing company under the Nazis. Gunnar Schnabel, the heirs’ Berlin lawyer, urged Sotheby’s to prove beyond a doubt that the painting was sold at market value in 1936 and that the family “would have wanted to carry out the sale even without Nazi rule.”

“Otherwise,” Schnabel wrote in a Nov. 12 email to Marco Toracca, the head of Sotheby’s restitution department, “no auction may take place.” In the email, made available to The New York Times, he said his client “is prepared to work toward a fair and just solution in the spirit of the 1998 Washington Principles,” international guidelines designed to help institutions and governments handling confiscated or Nazi-looted art.

“Blossoming Chestnut Trees” is part of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, which Philip Hook, a former Sotheby’s executive and author, described in the auction house’s announcement of the sale as “the stuff of legend: whispered about, kept from public view.” Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier of Buenos Aires began collecting Impressionist and modern art in the 1960s.
